title: The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build
gist: Agility Robotics cofounder Jonathan Hurst explains how safety, 20-hour shift endurance and certification requirements turned Digit 5 into a heavy, forklift-like humanoid built for warehouse bin handling. He frames the compromises as the price of commercial viability and a base for later agility.

insights.claim: Digit 5 is built to lift 23-kg bins to 1.75 m shelves, mirroring NIOSH lifting limits for human workers, and to run about 20 hours a day.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
entities: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health
insights.so_what: The spec is benchmarked to human occupational-safety norms, making ROI comparisons against labor hours direct.

insights.claim: Digit 5 runs 90 minutes and recharges in a 9-minute break via a dock delivering 240 A at 48 V, giving roughly 10% charging downtime and near-continuous operation.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Fast-charge docking, not battery chemistry alone, is what turns a humanoid into a multi-shift asset.

insights.claim: Battery and cooling occupy about 75 percent of Digit 5's torso and the robot exceeds 120 kg, which is why it can no longer run or jump.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Endurance requirements are driving humanoid mass and cost, so lighter, more agile designs will struggle to meet shift-length duty.
insights.quote: The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso

insights.claim: Hurst says any humanoid in a factory or warehouse either cannot lift the required weight, cannot last a whole shift, or is not safe to stand beside if it is not covered in sensors.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: This is a vendor's challenge to competitor demos; diligence on humanoid claims should test payload, shift duration and safety certification.
insights.quote: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift.

insights.claim: RoboFab in Salem, Oregon is a 70,000-square-foot facility with capacity for more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year, and the company targets tens of thousands of humanoid workers.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Stated capacity is a ceiling, not orders; scaling depends on customer demand and unit economics not disclosed here.

themes.theme: Safety and regulation as the binding constraint

insights.claim: In Digit 4 deployments, robots had to work behind physical barriers because of insurance and regulatory demands, which severely limited their usefulness.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Insurance and compliance, not capability, gated early humanoid deployment; whoever solves certified safety unlocks the addressable market.

insights.claim: Digit 5 is programmed to stop, set down its payload, sit on the floor and cut motor power as a person approaches, a conservative but verifiable approach to working beside humans.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Certifiable stop-and-sit behavior trades throughput for approval; pace of coexistence will track regulators, not model intelligence.
insights.quote: As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors

insights.claim: Safety took two years of design work and shaped nearly everything: leg and body shape, safety-rated sensors in protective housings, and isolated safety computers, all adding complexity, power draw, mass and size.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Safety architecture is a major cost and weight driver, favoring incumbents able to fund certification.

insights.claim: Compliance with European CE, North American UL and FCC emissions requirements were absolute product requirements that Hurst saw as tangential to his original vision.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Certification is a real moat and time sink for humanoid entrants.

themes.theme: Form follows function: humanoids converge on practical design

insights.claim: Digit 5 swaps the ostrich-like backward legs for human-like legs because the old ankle struck the ground when squatting, and knee and hip motors both contribute torque to stand up under load.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Task requirements (low lifts) are pushing humanoids toward human-like leg geometry, so convergence among competitors may be functional rather than imitation.

insights.claim: Hurst argues others have copied the human form without understanding its purpose, and that without matching function the point of the human form may be lost.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Skepticism of form-first humanoid designs suggests the field will be sorted by task performance, not looks.
insights.quote: Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose.

insights.claim: Digit 5 is described as feeling more like a forklift than a graceful humanoid, and it is the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: The first commercially viable humanoid may be a heavy industrial machine, implying an eventual price and size trajectory downward.

insights.claim: Digit 4 EVT's larger batteries and safety and compliance upgrades added enough mass to change its appearance and capabilities; the added head helped with antenna, camera placement and human interaction.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Compliance and connectivity requirements steadily add hardware.

themes.theme: Why bin handling first, and the road map

insights.claim: Agility picked bin handling because it needs two arms to lift bins high and legs to balance in narrow spaces, and varies too much between sites for single-purpose automation, yet is constrained enough to be viable.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Beachhead logic: humanoids win where task variety defeats fixed automation but scope stays bounded.

insights.claim: The road map extends from bins to item picking, machine tending, preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually assembly, using interchangeable tool interfaces and modular upgrades.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Expansion beyond bins is stated intent only; each step needs new manipulation capability and data.

insights.claim: Digit 5 is meant to be a source of data for future behavior training as well as a product, so early deployments double as data collection.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Fleet data may be the long-term moat, subsidizing thin early hardware margins.
insights.quote: It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.

insights.claim: Hurst calls Digit 5 the scaling moment and inflection point for Agility, where large-number deployments can begin.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: This is the founder's own claim and not yet evidenced by orders or deployment numbers.

insights.claim: Agility's cofounders began without a customer problem; they relied on belief that the technology would enable new possibilities and figured out the business later.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Technology-first humanoid ventures took about a decade to find a viable use case.

insights.claim: Cassie sold only 10 units at $250,000 each to universities and saturated the market for research bipedal robots.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: The research-robot market capped revenue near $2.5 million, so a pivot to commercial work was forced.

insights.claim: Early Digit deployments consumed enormous effort keeping them operational, which arguably eliminated any profit, though it kept the company learning.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Early humanoid unit economics are service-heavy, so margin expansion depends on reliability gains.

insights.claim: New executive leadership pushed major Digit 4 EVT changes on a compressed timeline, and mapping the first 10 use cases led to designing Digit 5 from scratch.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Leadership change from founder-led R&D to product discipline was the pivot; this pattern may recur across humanoid startups.

insights.claim: Cassie's hardware let researchers pioneer reinforcement learning for bipedal locomotion, in which a simulated robot's trained neural network controls the physical machine, underlying most dynamic legged-robot behavior today.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Agility's hardware seeded the control approach now used industry-wide.

insights.claim: Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the first commercially deployed humanoid at logistics provider GXO.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Named logistics customers give the first commercial humanoid reference accounts, though scale is not disclosed.

top_entities: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health
